Duhuo Jisheng Decoction Mitigates Osteochondral Degeneration in Knee Osteoarthritis through Modulation of Complement C3a/C3AR1-IKKβ-NF-κB Signaling
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is characterized by progressive osteochondral destruction driven by inflammatory and catabolic signaling, yet no approved structure-modifying pharmacotherapy currently exists. Duhuo Jisheng Decoction (DHJSD), a classic traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formula widely used for KOA, requires a clearer understanding of its mechanism of action. To address this, we integrated multiple approaches: a destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse model for initial therapeutic efficacy ( n = 3 per group), bulk articular cartilage RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) (Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO): GSE319157), network pharmacology, focused in vivo dose validation, in vitro dose-bridging assays, primary chondrocyte phospho-signaling assays, ex vivo complement activation, ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UHPLC-Q-TOF-MS) serum metabolomics, molecular docking and dynamics simulations, cellular target engagement assays cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), isothermal dose–response fingerprint CETSA (ITDRF-CETSA), and drug affinity responsive target stability (DARTS), and an in vivo C3a challenge-rescue experiment to interrogate the complement–IκB kinase beta (IKKβ)–nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) axis. DHJSD treatment was associated with preservation of osteochondral integrity and cartilage matrix homeostasis in DMM mice. The initial dose cohort (2, 4, and 8 g/kg/day) showed a non-monotonic efficacy pattern; an independent focused validation cohort centered on 4 g/kg/day confirmed this dose as the most consistent for mechanistic interrogation within the refined range tested. RNA-seq and network pharmacology identified a complement–NF-κB program as a DHJSD-responsive network. Bulk-cartilage complement C3a receptor 1 (C3AR1) transcript behavior including anchor-cohort reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) confirmation of the RNA-seq direction served as tissue-level contextual information, whereas mechanistic inference regarding C3AR1 was based on chondrocyte-level RT-qPCR, cartilage-localized protein expression, and downstream IKKβ–NF-κB signaling readouts. In primary chondrocytes, interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) induced C3 and C3AR1 transcripts and activated the IKKβ–inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa B alpha (IκBα)–v-rel reticuloendotheliosis viral oncogene homolog A (RelA, P65) cascade; DHJSD-medicated serum derived from the 4 g/kg dose most consistently attenuated these responses. Intra-articular C3a challenge partially blunted DHJSD-mediated protection, whereas IKKβ inhibition with BMS-345541 partially restored structural and signaling endpoints. UHPLC-Q-TOF-MS prioritized geniposidic acid (GA) as a blood-exposed candidate constituent, and CETSA, ITDRF-CETSA, and DARTS provided convergent cellular evidence supporting GA–IKKβ interaction, although direct biochemical affinity remains to be determined. Collectively, these data support a restrained mechanistic model in which DHJSD attenuates a complement-amplified IKKβ–NF-κB inflammatory circuit in experimental KOA. GA emerges as a prioritized candidate requiring pharmacokinetic (PK) and biochemical validation, and adequately powered dose-optimization studies are still warranted.

title: Mapping tryptophan metabolism: Unraveling its pathogenesis and therapeutic opportunities in asthma
abstract: Tryptophan (Trp) metabolism involves various bioactive compounds, primarily through the kynurenine (KYN), 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), and indole pathways, and is a key signaling molecule of the gut-lung axis. The imbalances of Trp metabolism are linked to asthma by abnormally regulating the biological function of immune cells. In clinical practice, the rate-limiting enzyme in Trp metabolism, indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), has significantly lower activity in allergic asthma, which is assessed by the concentration ratio of KYN to Trp and provides direction for the therapeutic intervention. Current intervention strategies for Trp metabolism in asthma include platelet 5-HT reuptake enhancers, such as tianeptine and melatonin (MT). At the same time, advancements in gut microbiota research have highlighted the potential of Trp-derived indole metabolites as practical approaches to alleviate relevant symptoms. Notably, multiple compounds and pharmaceuticals derived from distinct sources have been shown to target Trp metabolism for the treatment of asthma in some experiments. This review consolidates pharmaceuticals capable of modulating Trp metabolism and proposes prospective therapeutic strategies for asthma.

title: Tumor-Specific Degradation of EGFR and HER2 Mediated by a CD36-Directed Proteolysis Targeting Chimera
abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) are key oncogenic drivers in gastric and other solid tumors, yet the clinical benefit of conventional tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as lapatinib is limited by acquired resistance and incomplete pathway suppression. Proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) provide an event-driven strategy for simultaneous target elimination, but their translation is often constrained by on-target, off-tumor toxicity in normal tissues expressing basal levels of EGFR/HER2. Here, we developed a series of lapatinib-derived PROTACs that recruit the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) E3 ligase to induce dual degradation of EGFR and HER2. The lead compound, PROTAC-B7, showed superior antitumor activity to lapatinib, a selective EGFR degrader (PROTAC-A1), and a selective HER2 degrader (PROTAC-A2) in vitro and in vivo , but caused dose-limiting systemic toxicity. Mechanistically, we found that the fatty acid translocase CD36 mediates cellular uptake of fatty acid-conjugated PROTACs and is highly expressed in gastric cancer cells. Guided by this finding, we generated a second-generation molecule, PROTAC-B7.7, by conjugating PROTAC-B7 with a long-chain fatty acid. This modification enhanced CD36-dependent tumor cell uptake and intracellular accumulation, while reducing toxicity in normal cells with low CD36 expression. Consequently, PROTAC-B7.7 achieved more selective EGFR/HER2 degradation, stronger antitumor efficacy, and an improved therapeutic window in preclinical models. These findings establish CD36-mediated targeted delivery as a modular strategy to enhance the tumor selectivity and translational potential of PROTAC therapeutics.

title: Targeting aldolase B to disrupt the β-Catenin/TCF4 axis and inhibit hepatocellular carcinoma progression: A novel small-molecule therapeutic strategy
abstract: Aldolase B (ALDOB) acts as a tumor suppressor in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet its role in metastasis remains poorly defined, and the development of specific ALDOB modulators has posed a major challenge. Through genetic manipulation, this study establishes that ALDOB overexpression suppresses HCC proliferation and metastasis both in vitro and in vivo via dual mechanisms: inhibiting the pentose phosphate pathway and, following nuclear translocation, disrupting β-catenin/ transcription factor 4 (TCF4) interaction to repress oncogene transcription. An EED277-279AAA mutation disrupts the ALDOB–β-catenin interaction, thereby abolishing its anti-HCC effects. Leveraging these mechanisms, we identified 1-(3,4-dimethoxyphenyl)-3-(2-hydroxy-4,6-dimethoxyphenyl)propane-1,3-dione (MD33), a novel ALDOB modulator with potent anti-HCC activity. MD33 binds the ALDOB active sites, enhances ALDOB/β-catenin complex formation, promotes Akt dephosphorylation, and thereby effectively curbs tumor progression. These results highlight the central role of ALDOB in HCC pathogenesis and its potential as a therapeutic target amenable to both genetic and pharmacological intervention.

title: Structure-based mechanism elucidation and inhibitor discovery of bacteriophage depolymerases targeting Klebsiella pneumoniae KN1 serotype
abstract: Klebsiella phages are viruses targeting Klebsiella pneumoniae ( K. pneumoniae ). Due to long-term competition and co-evolution between them, the depolymerases of Klebsiella phages have developed the remarkable ability to selectively recognize and degrade capsule polysaccharide (CPS) on the corresponding host surface. Here we present the cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of two KN1-serotype CPS depolymerases, Dp42 at a resolution of 3.15 Å with C1 symmetry and at a higher resolution of 2.56 Å with C3 symmetry, and KN1dep at 2.58 Å resolution with C1 symmetry, respectively. The unique characteristics of KN1-serotype depolymerases have been revealed, which exists as a trimeric architecture consisting of an N-terminal domain, a β-helix domain, a β-sheet transition domain, and a C-terminal β-sandwich domain. Meanwhile, our findings provide a novel domain-swapping conformation for depolymerases. Furthermore, through comprehensive structural and functional analyses, we have uncovered the structural basis underlying the catalytic mechanisms involving the key amino acid residues Glu412, Asp452, Asp460, and Glu574, as well as the potential substrate-binding pocket. Additionally, we successfully identified two mild inhibitors of Dp42 via high-throughput screening, 1,2,3,6-tetragalloylglucose (TeGG) and its homologue 1,2,3,4,6-pentagalloylglucose (PGG). Furthermore, a comprehensive series of experimental assays was conducted to appraise the impacts exerted by Dp42 and its inhibitor TeGG and PGG. Overall, we provided more evidence for the interchain catalytic mode and drug antagonistic regulatory molecule of depolymerases. These results suggest that among this superfamily of depolymerases, a full-length phage depolymerase, which may offer advantages in stability and substrate engagement, rather than mini-depolymerases, holds greater potential as an effective therapeutic agent.

title: Knowledge graph-based screening for synergistic anticancer drug combinations
abstract: Combination therapies present a promising approach to overcome the rapid resistance and limited efficacy associated with monotherapies; however, identifying synergistic and safe combinations within the vast candidate space remains challenging. Here, we propose a dual-dimensional evaluation strategy for artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled discovery of synergistic drug pairs and develop KOMBO, a knowledge graph (KG)-driven deep learning (DL) framework that integrates multimodal drug features with cancer cell transcriptomes. By concurrently assessing combination efficacy (combination maximum effect, combo Emax > 50%) and synergy score (highest single agent (HSA) > 10%), KOMBO facilitates the prioritization of synergistic therapies and uncovers a previously untested extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK)-AKT serine/threonine kinase (AKT) co-targeting regimen, whose therapeutic potential is validated through biological experiments including acquired resistance models. KOMBO accurately identifies both known and novel synergistic combinations and exhibits heightened sensitivity for strongly synergistic pairs, demonstrating substantial practical utility. Leveraging KOMBO, we screened 6,786 unexplored drug combinations and selected high-priority candidates for experimental testing, revealing six combinations with synergistic effects across multiple cancer types. Notably, MK-2206 (inhibitor of AKT: AKTi) combined with SCH772984 (ERKi) showed pronounced in vitro and in vivo synergy in colorectal and triple-negative breast cancer models without inducing overt systemic toxicity, and effectively overcame acquired resistance to single agents, providing salient leads for future therapeutic innovation. Together, these findings highlight KOMBO as a powerful platform for accelerating rational combination therapy design and advancing synergistic cancer treatment strategies.

title: Membrane-anchored designer tissue inhibitor of matrix metalloproteinase (TIMP)-1 inhibits PD-L1 expression and shedding in triple-negative breast cancer via JAK-STAT-IRF1 signaling
abstract: Tissue inhibitor of matrix metalloproteinase-1 (TIMP-1) is the endogenous inhibitor of the matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) and a disintegrin and metalloproteinase (ADAM) families. This study aims to develop TIMP-1 as a therapeutic agent to suppress programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression in MDA-MB-231 breast adenocarcinoma cells. We engineered a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored TIMP-1 variant, designated "T1 PrαTACE ", with high affinity for ADAM10, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) converting enzyme (TACE) and membrane type 1-matrix metalloproteinases (MT1-MMP). Its effects on interferon gamma (IFN-γ)-mediated PD-L1 expression were evaluated using cell-based assays, molecular profiling and in vivo studies in NOD-scid gamma (NSG) mouse models. T1 PrαTACE effectively inhibits PD-L1 expression and shedding through dual mechanisms: suppressing IFN-γ-induced PD-L1 expression by downregulating Janus kinase 1 (JAK1)/signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) phosphorylation and reducing IFN regulatory factor 1 (IRF1) expression, and inhibiting the proteolytic activities of ADAM10, TACE and MT1-MMP to prevent soluble PD-L1 shedding. In NSG mice, MDA-MB-231 tumors expressing T1 PrαTACE showed slower growth, reduced serum PD-L1, diminished PD-L1 tissue staining and increased tumor necrosis. In T cell-preimmunized NSG mice, T1 PrαTACE -expressing tumors demonstrated significantly increased T cell infiltration and necrosis. Notably, T1 PrαTACE expression was associated with undetectable serum interleukin-6 (IL-6) due to suppression of the nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) pathway, suggesting a role in suppressing tumor-associated inflammation. In conclusion, T1 PrαTACE downregulates both membrane-bound and soluble PD-L1 by disrupting the JAK/STAT/IRF1 signaling axis and inhibiting metalloproteinase-mediated shedding, representing a promising biologic therapeutic candidate to inhibit tumor progression.

title: Zinc homeostasis in cancer: From dynamic regulation to therapeutic potential
abstract: Zinc is an essential trace element in the human body that exists as Zn 2+ and functions as not only a critical structural component of numerous proteins and enzymes but also a key signaling molecule involved in fundamental biological processes. Consequently, the dysregulation of Zn 2+ homeostasis is strongly associated with a broad spectrum of chronic diseases, including cancer. This review summarizes the mechanisms by which the dysregulation of Zn 2+ homeostasis is involved in cancer initiation and progression, with a focus on redox homeostasis, DNA damage repair, epigenetic modifications, and copper homeostasis. Moreover, this review elaborates on the biological effects of Zn 2+ homeostasis in the metabolic reprogramming of cancer cells, programmed cell death, cell cycle progression, and tumor microenvironment (TME) modulation. Additionally, on the basis of well-established mechanisms of drug resistance, including the upregulation of drug efflux pumps, the acquisition of cancer stem cell (CSC)-like properties, the suppression of apoptotic pathways, and intratumoral hypoxia, this review examines the potential role of zinc-associated agents in the mitigation of anticancer drug resistance. Finally, this review highlights the mechanisms of action and clinical potential of both conventional zinc-associated agents and novel zinc-associated nanotherapeutics for cancer therapy. Overall, this review advances the understanding of the multifaceted roles of Zn 2+ homeostasis in cancer and provides a theoretical basis for the development of related therapeutic strategies.

title: Therapeutic efficacy and mechanism of Turkish gall extract against porcine epidemic diarrhea virus
Polysaccharide A1 from bran-fried Atractylodes lancea enhances mucosal immunity via Faecalibaculum rodentium-mediated B-cell class-switch DNA recombination
abstract: ABSTRACT Chemotherapy-induced intestinal injury is a common adverse effect during tumor chemotherapy, which seriously impairs patients’ quality of life and may even lead to treatment interruption. Natural polysaccharides have been proven to alleviate intestinal damage by regulating the gut microbiota. As a dietary supplement, polysaccharide A1 from bran-fried Atractylodes lancea (FALP-A1) exhibits notable immunoregulatory and intestinal protective effects. However, the specific mechanisms underlying their modulation of gut microbiota and enhancement of intestinal mucosal immunity remain unclear. In this study, a chemotherapy-induced intestinal injury mouse model demonstrated that FALP-A1 significantly increased body weight, organ index, and blood cell count, upregulated the expression of intestinal tight junction proteins zona occludens-1 (ZO-1) and occludin, and repaired intestinal barrier function. Moreover, FALP-A1 elevated the number of IgA + B cells and the level of secreted immunoglobulin A (sIgA), thereby enhancing intestinal mucosal immunity. FALP-A1 also reversed gut microbiota dysbiosis and the decrease in short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) levels in treated mice, significantly enriching the SCFAs-producing probiotic Faecalibaculum rodentium ( F. rodentium ). The pseudo-sterile animal model and fecal microbiota transplantation experiments further confirmed that the protective effects of FALP-A1 on intestinal injury and mucosal immunity are dependent on the gut microbiota. Notably, transplantation of F. rodentium significantly improved pathological symptoms and enhanced mucosal immunity in chemotherapy-induced intestinal injury mice, further verifying the important role of this strain. Importantly, this study reveals that FALP-A1 promotes B-cell class switch DNA recombination (CSR) by upregulating the F. rodentium /SCFAs/activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AICDA)-sIgA axis, thereby potentiating intestinal mucosal immune responses. These findings provide a new perspective on the mechanisms by which natural polysaccharides alleviate intestinal injury and enhance mucosal immunity, and offer potential strategies for the clinical prevention and treatment of chemotherapy-induced intestinal injury.

title: Targeting HRG-mediated tubular epithelial cell-macrophage interplay restores the endogenous defense against calcium oxalate kidney stones
abstract: Dysfunction of renal macrophagic phagocytosis is closely associated with calcium oxalate (CaOx) kidney stone formation; however, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified the mechanism by which histidine-rich glycoprotein (HRG)-mediated communication between renal tubular epithelial cells (RTEC) and macrophages mediates the phagocytosis of stone crystals in clinical samples, in vivo , and in vitro stone models, using integrated proteomic and transcriptomic analyses coupled with biochemical experiments. Mechanistically, RTEC exhibited reduced HRG secretion under stone-forming conditions. Reduced HRG weakens interactions with FcgammaRI (FcγRI) receptors on macrophages, thereby inhibiting downstream phosphatidylinositol-3 kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (Akt) signaling pathways, which downregulates Ras-related protein rab-20 (RAB20) expression to diminish macrophage phagocytosis of crystals and reduces interleukin-33 (IL-33) expression to inhibit M2 polarization of macrophages. These combined effects impair macrophage crystal phagocytosis, ultimately promoting the formation of CaOx kidney stones. Additionally, we found that enhancing HRG expression significantly suppresses oxalate crystal aggregation in kidneys and renal injury induced by glyoxylate (Gly). Through pharmacological analysis, we also identified Hesperidin, a natural compound derived from traditional Chinese medicine and validated in mice, which may exert protective effects against CaOx kidney stones by targeting HRG. In summary, this study reveals an HRG-based RTEC-macrophage communication axis that regulates crystal macrophagic phagocytosis, providing new insights into the prevention and treatment of CaOx kidney stones.

title: Integrative pharmacokinetic profiling and single-cell transcriptomics unveil triptolide-celastrol combination as the key toxic driver in Tripterygium Glycosides Tablets-induced hepatic injury
abstract: Tripterygium glycosides tablet (TGT) demonstrates significant therapeutic efficacy in treating various autoimmune diseases. However, its clinical application is substantially limited by drug-induced liver injury, highlighting the need to identify the key toxic drivers and underlying mechanisms. To address this, we aimed to characterize the pharmacokinetic profiles and cellular heterogeneity-related toxic mechanisms of TGT-induced hepatic injury by integrating ultra-performance liquid chromatography coupled with quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry (UPLC-Q-TOF/MS), molecular docking, cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assay, an acute liver injury model, and single-cell RNA sequencing with cellular validation. Results showed that triptolide and celastrol, two major toxic components of TGT, were present in defined proportions and exhibited strong binding affinities to known hepatotoxic targets of TGT. Subsequent in vitro experiments confirmed that 0.34 μM celastrol synergistically enhanced the cytotoxicity of 0.01 μM triptolide in AML12 cells. Pharmacokinetic analysis and enzymatic activity assay revealed that celastrol inhibited the metabolic enzyme CYP3A4, thereby reducing triptolide degradation and increasing its hepatic accumulation. Histopathological evaluations verified that the liver injury patterns induced by the triptolide-celastrol combination were consistent with those caused by TGT, confirming their synergistic toxicity. Furthermore, single-cell transcriptomic analysis of TGT-induced acute liver injury in mice and cellular experiments identified that this compound combination activated hepatic stellate cell fibrogenesis, disrupted hepatocyte iron-lipid homeostasis, and triggered oxidative stress-apoptosis cascades in biliary epithelial cells. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the metabolic interaction and cellular cooperativity between triptolide and celastrol are pivotal drivers of TGT-induced hepatotoxicity, providing crucial insights into the mechanistic basis of TGT-related liver injury and potential strategies for clinical risk mitigation.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven De Novo Peptide Drug Design: Architectures, Pipelines, and Translational Challenges
abstract: In peptide drug design, function often emerges from the conformational ensemble encoded by a sequence and from how that ensemble engages a target. From this perspective, de novo peptide design can be viewed as an inverse problem of the sequence–structure–function relationship: starting from predefined functional and pharmacological objectives, one infers the required structural constraints and interfacial features and then generates candidate sequences that satisfy them. Achieving this goal requires a deeper mechanistic understanding of how peptide conformational ensembles, molecular recognition, and functional determinants jointly govern activity, as well as the ability to encode these principles in computational representations and models that are amenable to learning, explicit constraint, and optimization. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI)-driven approaches, including protein language models (pLMs), diffusion and latent diffusion models (LDM), conditional flow matching (CFM), and AI-assisted prediction and screening, are beginning to shift the field beyond sequence or structure generation toward function-oriented and controllable peptide design. At the same time, these advances have highlighted persistent bottlenecks in sequence–structure co-generation, conformational control in flexible systems, and interpretable multi-objective optimization. As de novo peptide design methods rapidly proliferate, technical routes are diversifying and benchmarking standards remain fragmented. This review therefore surveys recent progress in AI-driven generative architectures, control strategies, and emerging directions, with the aim of distilling reusable principles and providing a structured reference for reliable, translationally relevant functional peptide design.

title: Carbon Dots for Tumor Therapy: Mechanisms, Applications, and Future Perspectives
abstract: Carbon dots (CDs), as small zero-dimensional carbon-based nanomaterials, exhibit remarkable optical properties, high biocompatibility, and minimal toxicity. Their surfaces can be readily functionalized, enabling efficient drug loading, targeted modification, and stimulus-responsive release. CDs possess the unique capability to integrate both diagnostic and therapeutic functions, making them ideal carriers for the development of “theranostic” platforms. This paper systematically reviews recent research advances in CDs for tumor therapy, focusing on their mechanisms of action and potential applications as drug delivery systems, photothermal, photodynamic, and multimodal synergistic therapeutic platforms. At the same time, this paper also conducts an in-depth analysis of the challenges and limitations currently facing this field, including key issues such as biosafety, in vivo pharmacokinetics, large-scale synthesis standardization, and tumor microenvironment (TME) barriers. These advances represent a significant progression from fundamental research toward clinical translation.

title: Scrutinization on Docking against Individually Generated Target Pockets for each Ligand
abstract: Abstract The longstanding challenge of limited exploration in protein receptor conformational space continues to constrain the precision of molecular docking. Ensemble docking, which employs methods such as molecular dynamics simulations to generate multiple receptor conformations for docking, has improved accuracy but remains limited by incomplete sampling and an inability to fully account for ligand-induced fit. To address these limitations, we introduce the concept of individual docking, a novel approach that involves docking against receptor conformations generated individually for each ligand in the docking library. This approach has only very recently become feasible due to advances in protein structure prediction, in particular end-to-end protein-ligand complex prediction technologies. In this study, we performed individual docking on 27 targets from the DUD-E dataset, using a two-step protocol that integrates NeuralPLexer or AlphaFold3 for receptor conformation sampling, followed by physics-based docking. Our results reveal that individual docking with AlphaFold3 predictions yields more than a twofold improvement in enrichment factors compared to standard docking. Furthermore, individual docking recovers distinct sets of active ligands, thereby expanding the diversity of virtual screening hits. Detailed analyses of pocket and ligand conformations suggest several potential incompatibilities between deep learning-based and physics-based virtual screening tools.

title: Carbon-based nanoparticles from traditional black soybean oil: A novel nanotherapeutic strategy for atopic dermatitis via antioxidant modulation of pyroptosis
abstract: Black soybean oil (BSO) is a traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) for inflammatory skin disorders, yet its active basis remains unclear. Inspired by BSO preparation's similarity to carbon dot synthesis, we isolated fluorescent carbon-based nanoparticles (BSO-CNPs) from BSO. Analyses confirmed their characteristic nanostructure and fluorescence. Functionally, BSO-CNPs showed potent antioxidant activity, scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) and restoring cell viability under in vitro oxidative stress. In murine models of atopic dermatitis, topical BSO-CNPs alleviated clinical symptoms, reduced epidermal hyperplasia, suppressed mast cell infiltration, and downregulated inflammatory cytokines. Mechanistically, BSO-CNPs attenuate the NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3)/caspase-1/gasdermin D (GSDMD) pyroptosis pathway by suppressing mitochondrial ROS and stabilizing lysosomal function. Furthermore, BSO-CNPs demonstrated high biosafety in vitro and in vivo . These findings elucidate the material basis of BSO’s therapeutic effects and highlight BSO-CNPs as a novel nanotherapeutic candidate for atopic dermatitis, bridging traditional herbal medicine with modern nanomedicine.

title: Decoding the Black Box: Mapping Component-Target Links in Traditional Chinese Medicine
abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has long served as a valuable source for modern therapeutics. However, elucidating their precise mechanisms of action remains a major challenge. The inherent complexity of TCM, particularly the unclear relationship between its active substances and their molecular targets has significantly hindered its modernization and global acceptance. This review highlights recent advances in direct protein target identification technologies, including affinity-based and label-free strategies, and discusses their applicability in both monomeric compounds and complex TCM extracts. Importantly, we emphasize that while global targetome profiling can reveal extract-level protein interactions, it does not inherently resolve specific component-target relationships. To address this critical bottleneck, we outline a sequential analytical strategy that integrates global target identification with target-guided reverse ligand fishing technologies, offering a promising strategy to establish direct component-target correspondence within TCM complex mixtures. We further analyze the principles, representative applications, analytical strengths, and limitations of these approaches, and discuss future directions, including high-throughput interactomics and physiologically relevant models. By clarifying methodological integration strategies for mixture deconvolution, this review provides a practical roadmap for transitioning TCM research from empirical observations toward precise mechanistic decoding.

title: A PCA-enhanced NIR-2D-COS framework for in situ conformational characterization of subtle proteins in biopharmaceuticals
Regulatory effects of plant-derived natural products on non-cancer stem cells: Signaling pathways and molecular mechanisms
abstract: Non-cancer stem cells play a crucial role in tissue repair, regeneration, and homeostasis, making them key targets in regenerative medicine. Plant-derived natural products, as a treasure trove of bioactive compounds, have garnered extensive attention due to their remarkable advantages of structural diversity, high biocompatibility, and low side effects. Accumulating evidence indicates that these natural products can precisely regulate the proliferation, differentiation, self-renewal, and paracrine functions of non-cancer stem cells by intervening in key signaling pathways. However, a systematic and in-depth summary of the regulatory effects of plant-derived natural products on non-cancer stem cells, along with their underlying molecular mechanisms, remains lacking. This review focuses on plant-derived natural products and non-cancer stem cells (including mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), neural stem cells (NSCs), and hematopoietic stem cells, etc.). It systematically examines the regulatory effects of various plant-derived natural products on non-cancer stem cells and deeply deciphers the core signaling pathways involved. Furthermore, this review clarifies the complex molecular regulatory networks and key target molecules in the regulatory process. Finally, the challenges and prospects of plant-derived natural products for regulating non-cancer stem cells in clinical applications are discussed. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive theoretical basis for in-depth research on plant-derived natural products and their clinical applications in non-cancer stem cell-based regenerative medicine.

title: Mechanosensitive ion channels: Shedding light on their functions and mechanisms in digestive system diseases
abstract: Mechanosensitive ion channels (MeSICs) are a class of ion channels that sense mechanical signals arising from changes in membrane tension, including extracellular stretch, shear stress and osmotic pressure fluctuations. These signals can activate MeSICs, which subsequently convert mechanical stimuli into electrochemical signals, thereby reconfiguring intracellular pathways and regulating downstream gene expression. In the gastrointestinal tract, MeSICs regulate intestinal motility as well as intestinal barrier function and permeability, while in the liver and pancreas, they participate in modulating bile and pancreatic juice secretion. However, dysregulation of MeSICs is closely associated with a broad range of digestive system disorders. Notably, accumulating evidence demonstrates that MeSICs participate in inflammatory diseases of the digestive system by modulating the activation and function of diverse immune cells. Their regulatory effects primarily encompass inflammatory cytokine secretion, cell differentiation, migration and apoptosis. Current studies mainly focus on single channels or individual diseases in the digestive system. In this review, we systematically summarize the functions and biological mechanisms of different MeSICs across the spectrum of digestive system diseases, from inflammation regulation to tumorigenesis, and highlight their therapeutic potential. Together, these insights provide a promising new direction for targeting mechano-chemical signaling in the treatment of related disorders.

title: Plasma multi-omics profiling reveals unique precursors of post-COVID cognitive decline during clinical recovery in older patients
abstract: Older patients with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) face substantial challenges from post-COVID cognitive decline (PCCD); however, the early clinical recovery phase of these sequelae remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we conducted a prospective cohort study of 47 older patients with COVID-19 aged ≥ 75 years. Plasma samples collected during hospitalization were subjected to proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic analyses using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Cognitive function was assessed at baseline and 10–12 months post-infection, to identify early recovery-phase molecular features associated with later cognitive outcomes. The results indicated that despite viral clearance, older individuals exhibited persistent alterations in plasma molecular features related to immune processes and neurovascular unit (NVU) function. Further follow-up at 10–12 months identified aging-specific early factors closely associated with long-term PCCD, including coordinated alterations in immune and inflammatory processes, extensive plasma exposure of markers indicative of NVU and skin epithelial barrier, and metabolic perturbations. Lipidomic and clinical data further corroborated these observations. A multilayer feature selection framework identified candidate biomarkers across multi-omics and clinical layers, and exploratory predictive models demonstrated discriminative performance for cognitive outcomes at 10–12 months. Cross-cohort comparison revealed partially consistent pathway-level alterations. In addition, a set of “prognostic-cognitive decline” molecules exhibiting cross-stage expression patterns was identified, suggesting persistent molecular perturbations associated with disease progression. Our findings provide systematic multi-omics insights into the early identification and underlying molecular mechanisms of cognitive sequelae in older patients with COVID-19.

title: Targeting U2-Type Spliceosome by Quercetin Suppresses EZH2 Oncogenic Isoforms in Lung Adenocarcinoma
abstract: EZH2, a key regulatory component of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), is involved in the epigenetic inheritance associated with the development of various tumors, including lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). While multiple splice variants of EZH2 have been identified, the oncogenic mechanisms of isoforms generated through its alternative splicing in LUAD remain unclear. The U12-type alternative spliceosome, consisting of U2AF1, U2AF2, and SRSF3, was found to mediate the splicing of EZH2 pre-mRNA and promote the formation of EZH2-T1. The natural flavonoid quercetin, exhibited potent anticancer effects. It acted as a small-molecule inhibitor of SRSF3, disrupted the formation of the U12-type alternative spliceosome, and suppressed the generation of EZH2-T1, all critical for its anticancer activity. Furthermore, transcriptome sequencing identified downstream targets influenced by quercetin. Experimental evidence showed that quercetin reduced the promoter-binding activity of EZH2-T1 to PCDH20 and inhibited its transcriptional repression of the tumor suppressor PCDH20. These findings highlight the potential of small-molecule compounds in modulating alternative gene splicing and provide valuable insights for developing novel therapeutic strategies against LUAD.

title: Bioactive materials for sepsis-induced coagulopathy therapeutics: Preclinical advances and clinical prospects
abstract: Sepsis-induced coagulopathy (SIC) is a severe complication of sepsis, characterized by dysregulated coagulation, immune overactivation, and microvascular injury. These interconnected pathological processes often lead to widespread thrombosis and multi-organ failure. While conventional anticoagulant and anti-inflammatory therapies offer partial relief, they frequently fall short in addressing the complex pathophysiology of SIC and may lack safety and personalization. Recent advances in lipid-based carriers, polymeric systems, and biomimetic constructs have demonstrated the ability to restore immune-coagulation balance, alleviate microvascular damage, and reduce oxidative stress in preclinical models. Addressing these barriers will require biomarker-guided patient phenotyping, integrated diagnostic-therapeutic platforms, and interdisciplinary clinical validation.

title: Agentic Spatial Digital Twins in Pharmacology: Decoding 4D Drug Response Dynamics within the Tissue Microenvironment
abstract: Traditional clinical and systems pharmacological frameworks often oversimplify the complex tissue microenvironment (TME). These population-averaged compartmental assumptions are fundamentally limited in accurately capturing the dynamic physical barriers governing localized drug bioavailability and continuous pharmacodynamic (PD) transitions across diverse spatial niches. This review systematically introduces the paradigm of agentic spatial digital twins (ASDT)—a computational framework designed to transform static spatiotemporal multi-omics atlases into generative, physics-constrained simulation platforms. Our objective is to provide a standardized, actionable roadmap empowering computational biologists, systems pharmacologists, and translational clinicians to transition from static tissue snapshots toward four-dimensional, continuous-time cellular trajectory extrapolations under combinatorial pharmacological perturbations. We deconstruct the functional orchestration of emerging single-cell and spatial foundation networks—specifically highlighting EpiAgent for physical chromatin accessibility gating and Nicheformer for multicellular neighborhood cross-talk modeling. To bridge the translational gap between computational hypotheses and empirical validation, we delineate the “silicon-carbon bridge”—a closed-loop infrastructure that continuously cross-validates in silico mechanistic reasoning against automated, microfluidic patient-derived organoid (PDO) platforms. Crucially, we dissect the mathematical necessity of embedding fundamental mass-action kinetics and thermodynamic continuity equations directly into generative objective functions to structurally mitigate algorithmic drift and biological hallucinations. By detailing the structural integration of clinical survival metrics as a baseline alignment constraint, this review aims to foster a consensus for validated virtual tissue standards within the scientific community. Ultimately, the ASDT paradigm serves as a technical catalyst for future regulatory developments, accelerating high-throughput lead combination discovery, reducing preclinical candidate attrition, and providing an empirically robust foundation for individualized precision dosing.

title: TWN-Align: Bridging hydration topology and fragment-based drug design for high-throughput kinase fragment prioritization
Apoptotic Bodies: Formation Mechanisms, Source-Dependent Heterogeneity, and Therapeutic Potential
abstract: Apoptotic bodies (ApoBDs) are membrane-bound vesicular structures generated during the late stages of programmed cell death. They were traditionally regarded as inert cellular debris that is removed by phagocytes, but increasing evidence suggests that ApoBDs are not simply passive byproducts of apoptosis. Instead, they can participate in intercellular communication and contribute to the maintenance of tissue homeostasis. Their formation involves coordinated cytoskeletal remodeling, membrane blebbing, and vesicle fragmentation, which together package diverse nuclear and cytoplasmic components into membrane-enclosed structures. Recent studies further indicate that the composition and biological effects of ApoBDs are closely related to their cellular origin. ApoBDs derived from stem cells, immune cells, and tumor cells may carry different cargos and exhibit distinct functional tendencies, leading to different effects on recipient cells in different biological contexts. These source-related differences not only reflect the heterogeneity of ApoBDs, but also distinguish them from other extracellular vesicle subtypes. In this review, we summarize recent progress in the mechanisms of apoptotic body formation and discuss how cellular origin influences their cargo composition, recognition, uptake, and downstream biological effects. We also discuss their potential relevance in tissue repair, immune regulation, disease intervention, and biomarker-related applications, while highlighting current limitations in this field, including methodological inconsistency, insufficient standardization, and the challenges that still restrict their further translational application.

title: Tectorigenin reprograms macrophages through targeting OXCT1-mediated ketone metabolism to suppress IFN-I signaling and ameliorate myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury
abstract: Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury persists as a pivotal unresolved bottleneck in treating acute myocardial infarction. Post-reperfusion inflammation, driven by macrophage metabolic and functional reprogramming, exacerbates this injury. Tectorigenin (TEC), an active component of Belamcanda chinensis , exerts marked cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury by targeting macrophage-mediated inflammation. TEC significantly improved cardiac function, reduced infarct size, and suppressed cardiomyocyte apoptosis. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) identified the type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling pathway as a key target. Mechanistically, TEC reduced macrophage reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and upregulated the transcriptional repressor basic helix-loop-helix family member e41 (BHLHE41). BHLHE41 subsequently suppressed expression of the cytosolic RNA sensor melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5), encoded by IFN induced with helicase C domain 1 ( Ifih1 )), thereby blocking downstream activation of TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) and IFN regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) to reduce IFN-β production. Moreover, multiple orthogonal assays identified 3-oxoacid CoA-transferase 1 (OXCT1), a crucial enzyme involved in ketone body metabolism, as a direct target of TEC, with TRP413 serving as the critical binding residue. This interaction promotes lysosomal degradation of OXCT1 and elevates intracellular ketone body levels, which enhance Bhlhe41 messenger RNA (mRNA) stability and inhibit MDA5-dependent IFN-I signaling. Exogenous ketone body supplementation mimicked these effects, while genetic knockdown of Oxct1 or Bhlhe41 confirmed their pivotal roles in regulating macrophage activation. Collectively, this study identifies a novel macrophage OXCT1-BHLHE41-MDA5 axis modulating IFN-I-driven inflammation during I/R injury, establishes TEC as a promising therapeutic agent, and highlights ketone metabolism as a potential cardioprotective target.

title: Editorial Board
Discovery of therapeutic agents targeting CKAP4 for kidney fibrosis using drug repositioning
abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) characterized by the progressive loss of renal, represents a significant global health challenge. Central to CKD progression is kidney fibrosis, an irreversible process marked by the accumulation of extracellular matrix proteins. The development of effective antifibrotic therapies is thus crucial for improving patient outcomes. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of bulk RNA sequencing data from unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO) and folic acid (FA)-induced nephropathy mice models, combined with single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) to explore cellular heterogeneity and molecular mechanisms of kidney fibrosis. Differential gene expression analysis, gene co-expression network (CN) analysis, time-series clustering, and cell marker analysis were employed to identify core fibrosis-related genes. Our analyses revealed a set of 37 core fibrosis-related genes which are largely associated with inflammation and immune response and contributed to the production of extracellular matrix (ECM), with Ckap4 standing out as a key marker of kidney fibrosis. In vivo experiments demonstrated that knockdown of Ckap4 significantly reduced kidney fibrosis in UUO mice, as evidenced by decreased collagen deposition and improved renal function. Additionally, the repurposed small molecule drugs, especially CGP-60474, showed promising antifibrotic effects, further highlighting the potential of Ckap4 as a therapeutic target.

title: A comprehensive narrative review of artificial intelligence applications in drug discovery and pharmaceutical practice
abstract: This comprehensive narrative review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is being applied in drug discovery and pharmacy practice. In pharmaceutical research, methods such as machine learning (ML) and neural networks help predict key physicochemical properties, optimize pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles, and support early toxicity assessment. These applications can accelerate the identification of promising drug candidates and make the design and conduct of clinical trials more efficient and cost-conscious. In clinical practice, AI supports medication management by automating prescription verification, assisting in dose selection, and detecting adverse drug reactions (ADRs) close to real time. AI based clinical decision support systems are increasingly used to reduce medication errors and to monitor patient adherence to treatment. High income countries are also deploying AI driven platforms in digital therapeutics, pharmaceutical supply chain management, and real time drug performance monitoring. Despite this progress, several barriers limit wider adoption. Biased or unrepresentative training data, the opaque “black box” nature of many models, and fragmented regulatory requirements remain major challenges. Ethical concerns related to patient privacy, data security, and algorithmic fairness require robust governance frameworks. Furthermore, the inherent complexity of biological systems and the shortage of professionals trained to interpret AI outputs constrain effective implementation. Overall, the potential of AI to reshape pharmaceutical science is substantial, but its long-term impact will depend on addressing regulatory and ethical issues and strengthening collaboration among researchers, healthcare professionals, and policy makers.

title: A Multisource-Integrated Atlas of Adverse Reactions Associated with Immunological Agents
abstract: Immunological agents are vital for treating cancer and autoimmune diseases, yet their therapeutic potential is limited by complex multi-organ adverse drug reactions (ADRs). Existing databases lack comprehensive integration of real-world ADR patterns, quantitative risk metrics, and mechanistic insights. To address this, the comprehensive atlas of immunological agents and adverse drug reactions (IMADRD) was developed. IMADRD provides three core data components: (1) ADR occurrence features, leveraging 194,035 clinical and real-world datasets; (2) quantitative metrics, featuring 18,305 unique ADRs across 27 system organ classes (SOCs), including 75,425 incidence records, 15,248 severity annotations, and 131,494 signal intensities; and (3) Drug-ADR-protein interaction networks, connecting 315 drugs, 2586 ADRs, 2361 proteins, and 22,892 associations. Then, targeted analysis of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) further validates IMADRD’s practical utility. Through systematic evaluation of approximately 100 ICIs, IMADRD accurately identifies high-risk SOCs and uncovers rare but severe neuropsychiatric risks. More notably, IMADRD enables quantitative assessment of drug similarity through ADR profile comparisons, providing clinicians with evidence-based guidance for selecting alternative therapies or avoiding known high-risk agents. Overall, by integrating and analyzing multidimensional data, IMADRD advances our understanding of the biological mechanisms of ADRs and supports the development of personalized immunotherapy regimens. IMADRD is freely accessible at http://imadrd.bipslab.com .

title: Relative quantitation strategy of glycans in tocilizumab labeled based on mass spectrometry probes d0/d15-CEBTPP: Monitoring glycan changes in rat serum
abstract: Glycosylation is crucial for the effector functions of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies (mAbs). However, the specific glycoprofile of tocilizumab, a humanized anti-interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor mAb, remains inadequately characterized in the current literature. To address this, we designed and synthesized a novel pair of stable isotope-labeled mass spectrometry (MS) probes: d0/d15-[4-(1-carboxyethyl)phenyl]methyl-triphenylphosphonium (d0/d15-CEBTPP). Featuring a permanent positive charge, these probes not only significantly enhance the ionization efficiency and detection sensitivity of glycans in MS positive-ion mode, but also effectively neutralize the intrinsic negative charge of sialic acid residues, thereby substantially improving the structural stability of acidic glycans during analysis. Consequently, a novel relative quantification strategy for glycans was established by coupling d0/d15-CEBTPP isotopic labeling with ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-high-resolution MS (UHPLC-HRMS). Methodological validation using a sialoglycopeptide (SGP) model demonstrated excellent linearity ( R 2 = 0.9990), reproducibility (coefficient of variation (CV) = 3.50%), and accuracy (relative error (RE) = 0.76%) across a 10-fold molar mixing range. Application of this strategy to the comprehensive characterization of tocilizumab successfully identified 23 N-glycans, including 14 fucosylated and 7 sialylated glycoforms. Furthermore, the method was successfully applied in a rat model, precisely tracking the dynamic fluctuations of targeted serum glycan levels from 2 min to 36 h post-administration. Overall, this study establishes a robust strategy for the efficient and reliable relative quantification of trace glycans in complex biological matrices without relying on glycan standards. This work offers a powerful analytical tool for comprehensive glycosylation evaluation in biopharmaceuticals and disease-related comparative glycomics.

title: In-depth tyrosine phosphoproteomics: From analytical method development towards application to gefitinib resistance study
abstract: Tyrosine phosphorylation (pTyr) plays critical roles in diverse physiological and pathological processes. Mass spectrometry (MS)-based strategies have been developed for mapping pTyr proteome. Nonetheless, ultradeep characterization of pTyr signaling is still hindered by inherently low abundance and highly dynamic range. Here, we designed a sensitive and cost-efficient workflow combining Src homology 2 (SH2) superbinder-based enrichment with data independent acquisition (DIA)-based MS analysis for tyrosine phosphoproteomics. By applying the hybrid DIA (hybDIA) search strategy, this approach identified over 7000 high-confidence pTyr sites, achieving the deepest coverage of the tyrosine phosphoproteome in a single measurement reported thus far. Moreover, this approach showed superior performance on detection sensitivity, data completeness, quantitative robustness, and accuracy. Applied to gefitinib resistance in non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLCs), multiple canonical resistance pathways, including phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K-AKT), epidermal growth factor (EGF) receptor-tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI) resistance, and erythroblastic leukemia viral oncogene B (ERBB) pathways, were significantly enriched, confirming the reliability and applicability of our analytical workflow. In addition, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis and neurotrophin signaling pathways showed high potential to participate in gefitinib resistance. In light of these findings, drug combination experiments further demonstrated that inhibitors of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) or tropomyosin receptor kinase (TRK) significantly enhanced the therapeutic efficacy of gefitinib. Phosphorylation at nuclear envelope membrane protein 1 (NEMP1) Ser368, ribosomal protein S6 kinase b1 (RPS6KB1) Ser441/Thr444, and cortactin (CTTN) Tyr154 showed potentially important roles in gefitinib resistance. Functional rescue assay of NEMP1 Ser368 and RPS6KB1 Ser441/Thr444 further demonstrated that phosphorylation-defective mutant, compared to the phosphomimetic mutant, significantly enhanced the sensitivity of resistant cell to gefitinib. Collectively, this study provides a powerful tool for Tyr phosphoproteomics, facilitating mechanistic insights into the EGFR-TKI resistance in NSCLC.

title: Traditional Chinese medicine-derived carbon dots: A new horizon in green nanotheranostics
abstract: Bridging the inherent bioactivity of botanical precursors with the tunable physicochemical properties of nanoscale particles, traditional Chinese medicine-derived carbon dots (TCM-CDs) have emerged as a promising innovative platform in sustainable nanotheranostics. Synthesized via eco-friendly routes such as hydrothermal or microwave-assisted carbonization, these nanomaterials exhibit “pharmacological inheritance,” a notable phenomenon wherein bioactive moieties from precursors (e.g., polyphenols, alkaloids, and polysaccharides) are partially retained or structurally transformed, contributing to their observed therapeutic activities. By combining structural features including ultrasmall size (<10 nm) and tunable optical properties with intrinsic bioactivity, TCM-CDs show promising preclinical potential in imaging-guided therapy, anti-inflammation, oncology, hemostasis, and tissue regeneration. Despite this considerable preclinical promise, the transition of TCM-CDs from bench to bedside remains impeded by critical bottlenecks, including batch-to-batch heterogeneity, lack of standardized quality control (QC) protocols, suboptimal delivery precision, and incomplete understanding of their long-term biosafety and underlying molecular mechanisms. Herein, we systematically review the latest advancements in the synthesis, purification, and biomedical applications of TCM-CDs. To facilitate future clinical translation, we highlight that integrating multi-omics technologies with precisely controlled manufacturing processes represents a critical path toward advancing the next generation of herbal-derived nanomedicines.

title: Targeting heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C reprograms macrophage metabolism to promote phagocytosis and suppress acute myeloid leukemia
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is driven by complex cellular interactions within the bone marrow microenvironment, in which tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and leukemia stem cells (LSCs) play essential regulatory roles. This study investigated how the N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) reader protein heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein C (HNRNPC) modulates macrophage function and influences AML progression. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) identified sixteen distinct cell types and revealed enhanced macrophage communication with other cell populations, accompanied by reduced interactions involving M1 macrophages in AML. Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses identified HNRNPC as a key m 6 A-related regulator of macrophage activity through the modulation of metabolic pathways. In vitro , silencing of HNRNPC increased tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle activity and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, thereby promoting M1 polarization, enhancing tumor cell recognition and phagocytosis, and strengthening antitumor immune responses. In vivo , macrophage-specific deletion of HNRNPC significantly suppressed tumor growth and extended survival in AML-bearing mice. Collectively, the findings identify HNRNPC as a central mediator linking m 6 A modification to macrophage metabolic reprogramming and immune activation, offering a promising potential for therapeutic intervention in AML.

title: Matairesinol: A review of natural sources, synthesis, pharmacological properties, pharmacokinetics and toxicity
abstract: Matairesinol (MAT) is a prominent bioactive dibenzylbutyrolactone lignan that exhibits a broad spectrum of pharmacological properties, including anti-inflammatory, anticancer, antioxidant, antidiabetic, and neuroprotective activities. Prevalent in dietary plants and medicinal herbs, MAT modulates diverse cellular pathways by regulating cytokine production, apoptotic cascades, and core metabolic enzymes, while in silico profiling confirms its high-affinity interaction with multiple oncogenic and inflammatory targets. Pharmacokinetically, MAT is metabolized extensively to enterolignans, enterodiol (ED), and enterolactone (EL), all of which are key to its bioactivity and are mediated by the microbiome. Toxicological evaluations reveal a good selectivity index, particularly in oncological models. However, new data highlight the need to address genotype-specific safety concerns. The review summarizes available information on the natural sources, synthesis methods, pharmacological properties, pharmacokinetics, and toxicological data of MAT, and provides a comprehensive overview of its therapeutic potential.

title: Stimuli-responsive polymer carrier delivery of natural products for inflammation treatment: A review
abstract: Inflammation, particularly chronic inflammation, underlies the pathogenesis of numerous major diseases; therefore, anti-inflammatory therapy represents a highly promising strategy for their prevention and treatment. Owing to their multi-target activities, low toxicity, and remarkable chemical diversity, natural products exhibit immense potential in combating inflammation. Although they have garnered widespread attention in the treatment of inflammatory diseases due to their potent efficacy and favorable safety profiles, their clinical application remains largely restricted by inherent physicochemical limitations. To systematically address these challenges, this review reclassifies naturally derived pharmacologically active substances into three primary categories, comprehensively analyzing the specific bottlenecks each category encounters during clinical translation. Driven by these application demands, this article highlights the critical role of stimuli-responsive polymeric carriers in overcoming these limitations. By integrating principles from materials science and pharmaceutics, the review elaborates on how morphological strategies of polymeric matrices can be tailored to address the specific physicochemical deficits of these drugs, thereby facilitating precise targeted delivery to lesion sites. Furthermore, considering the increasing complexity of modern carrier design, this review prospectively introduces the concept of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted design, discussing emerging applications of AI in accelerating natural product screening and the rational design of smart delivery systems. Ultimately, this review underscores that stimuli-responsive polymeric carriers can not only effectively circumvent the drawbacks of conventional drug administration but also significantly reduce required dosages and adverse side effects via precisely controlled release. Consequently, this work establishes a robust theoretical foundation and outlines novel developmental trajectories for next-generation therapeutic strategies against inflammatory diseases.

title: Pharmacological promotion of p62-mediated Keap1 autophagic degradation by Atractylenolide III ameliorates hepatic steatosis and senescence in alcohol-induced liver injury
abstract: Alcoholic liver disease (ALD) is a chronic liver condition worldwide that is driven by an annual increase in alcohol consumption. This study aimed to investigate the impact of atractylenolide III (AT-III) in ALD. Male C57BL/6N mice fed an ethanol (EtOH)-containing liquid diet and EtOH-induced AML12 cells were used systematically to assess the effect of AT-III on liver injury using histological and biochemical assays. Additionally, the regulatory effect of AT-III on nuclear factor erythroid-2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) was validated in Nrf2 −/− mice. Molecular docking, cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA), surface plasmon resonance (SPR), quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR), Western blotting, immunofluorescence, immunohistochemistry, and coimmunoprecipitation analyses were employed to demonstrate the effects of AT-III on ALD. This study found that AT-III could ameliorate biochemical and pathological liver injury in ALD mice. Moreover, AT-III inhibited oxidative stress and cellular senescence both in vivo and in vitro by activating the adenosine monophosphate (AMP)-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/Nrf2 pathway. Importantly, molecular docking, CETSA, and SPR analyses demonstrated that AT-III had a favorable binding ability with AMPK and that the AMPK inhibitor compound C (CC) or inhibition of Nrf2 markedly abolished the inhibitory effects of AT-III on lipid accumulation and cellular senescence in EtOH-induced AML12 cells and Nrf2 −/− mice. Mechanistically, AT-III promoted p62-dependent autophagic degradation of Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1) and thereby induced Nrf2 translocation into the nucleus. In conclusion, the protective role of AT-III against EtOH-induced ALD was mediated by AMPK/Nrf2/Keap1-dependent inhibition of cellular senescence, suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy for ALD.

title: RASSF10/FBXW11/WASH1 axis attenuates endosomal sorting-dependent autophagy and lipid metabolism to enhance docetaxel sensitivity in gastric cancer
abstract: Docetaxel (DTX) resistance and heterogeneous patient responses limit its clinical benefit in gastric cancer (GC). Although drug-induced adaptive survival programs drive therapeutic resistance, whether DTX activates such programs and how they are regulated remain unclear. Here, we investigated Ras association domain family member 10 (RASSF10), a tumor suppressor frequently epigenetically silenced, as a regulator of DTX sensitivity. Integrated analyses of neoadjuvant/conversion therapy cohorts, patient-derived organoids, and multi-omics datasets showed reduced RASSF10 expression in DTX non-responders and associations with poorer clinical outcomes. RASSF10 sensitized GC cells to DTX by suppressing stress-induced autophagy and lipid metabolic reprogramming. Mechanistically, RASSF10 recruited the E3 ligase F-box and WD repeat domain-containing 11 (FBXW11) to promote K48-linked ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homologue 1 (WASH1) at lysine 220, a process enhanced by DTX exposure. RASSF10 loss stabilized WASH1, promoting WASH1-dependent endosomal trafficking of autophagy-related 9A (ATG9A) cluster of differentiation 36 (CD36) to support autophagosome biogenesis and lipid droplet formation, respectively. Plasma RASSF10 promoter methylation showed potential as an exploratory biomarker for DTX response, and cyclic arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (cRGD)-modified liposomal recombinant RASSF10 improved DTX response preclinically. These findings identify RASSF10 as a regulator of DTX-induced adaptive autophagy and lipid metabolic reprogramming in GC and support its potential as both an exploratory biomarker and a therapeutic sensitization strategy.

title: Core regulatory pathways of natural products in anti-aging: Research progress at molecular, cellular, and systemic levels
abstract: The global aging population is triggering a public health crisis in age-related diseases. Aging is a complex biological process that encompasses molecular, cellular, and systemic levels. For a long time, synthetic drugs used in anti-aging strategies have faced limitations due to safety concerns, the narrow focus of single-target approaches, and clinical translation barriers. Natural products, with their multi-target regulatory effects and relatively low toxicity, hold significant potential as ideal agents for modulating the aging network. However, an integrated, mechanism-driven framework linking their effects to aging networks across biological scales is still lacking. Therefore, this review systematically summarizes eight core mechanisms of natural products in anti-aging: mitigating oxidative stress, preserving telomere integrity, regulating autophagy, sustaining mitochondrial dynamics, regulating apoptosis, suppressing chronic inflammation, restoring immune homeostasis, and reshaping the gut microbiome. Based on these interconnected mechanisms, we propose a hierarchical analytical framework that integrates natural products, multi-target regulation, multi-level anti-aging mechanisms, and aging-related diseases. This framework highlights the “natural product-multi-target regulation-multi-level mechanism-aging-related disease” paradigm and provides an organized perspective for understanding the systemic anti-aging effects of natural products. In summary, this integrative framework aims to offer a theoretical foundation for developing advanced and precise anti-aging strategies that support the goal of global healthy aging.

title: Multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging for molecular profiling and precision-targeted pharmacotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma
The isoelectric point as a design parameter: From charge characterization to programmable biomedicine
abstract: The isoelectric point ( p I) is a key surface physicochemical parameter of amphoteric molecules and various functional nanomaterials that directly governs their stability, solubility, and biological interactions. Recently, the role of p I has shifted from a traditional characterization tool to an active design parameter. This review systematically highlights representative research advances in this evolution. It first revisits the fundamental concepts and classical methods for p I determination and then focuses on its roles as a programmable design parameter in emerging applications, including modulating drug stability, immunogenicity, and pharmacokinetics; enhancing quality control; optimizing drug delivery systems, diagnostic probe design, and clinical assays; and advancing computational tools for p I prediction. Based on the foregoing analysis, this review aims to elucidate how p I-based design can transform p I from a mere physicochemical metric into a core engine for next-generation biomedical innovation, advancing personalized therapies and the development of advanced biologics.

title: An integrative PRISM framework for screening active herbal constituents, using Farfarae Flos in microplastic-induced lung injury as an application case
abstract: Herbal drugs from traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) have shown promising efficacy in polystyrene microplastics (PS-MPs) induced inhalation lung injury, however, challenges remain in how to discover the effective compounds based on precise pathological mechanisms. We present pipeline for rapid in silico medicine screening (PRISM), an integrated four-module computational framework designed for mechanism-driven screening of active compounds in the preselected herbal drugs in the context of specific disease pathology. As a proof-of-concept application, PRISM was applied to Farfarae Flos (FF) against PS-MPs-induced inhalation injury. PRISM integrates four modules, single-cell/bulk transcriptomic analysis, gene expression profile predictor on chemical structures (GPS) based drug screening, unified in silico cellular dynamics and drug discovery framework (UNAGI)-based virtual perturbation, and unified stacking ensemble for target activity prediction (UNISTACK) target activity prediction, into a unified pipeline for bioactive compound screening from herbs. PRISM identified cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2, encoded by PTGS2 ) and 5-lipoxygenase (5-LOX, encoded by ALOX5 ) co-upregulated in a pathogenic neutrophil subpopulation as core targets, supported the therapeutic potential of FF through transcriptional reversal of the disease genes, predicted that FF may redirect pathogenic neutrophil states through PTGS2/ALOX5 -related perturbation, and predicted 15 potential dual-target inhibitors. In vivo experiments, pseudotargeted metabolomics, and in vitro enzyme inhibition assays confirmed the therapeutic effects of FF and the key bioactive components from the computational predictions. In summary, PRISM provides a practical computational framework for evaluating the pharmacological potential of herbal medicines and prioritizing bioactive constituents, and we demonstrated its application using FF in microplastic-induced lung injury.

title: Human Dosimetry of Therapeutic Radiopharmaceuticals Using Allometrically Scaled Preclinical Pharmacokinetics Integrated with a Single Time-Point Patient Image
The “one-stone-multiple-birds” strategy of salvianolic acids against ischemia-reperfusion injury: Multi-organ protection (beyond cardio) via common & specific mechanisms
abstract: Ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury poses a significant global health challenge, characterized by multi-organ involvement (such as heart, brain, intestine, and kidneys) and interconnected inflammatory, oxidative, and apoptotic signaling pathways. This complexity limits the efficacy of single-target synthetic drugs. Salvianolic acids (SACs), the major water-soluble components of Salvia miltiorrhiza (SM) with SAC A (Sal A) and SAC B (Sal B) as the predominant constituents, exert multi-organ protective effects through a “one-stone-multiple-birds” strategy. Their core mechanisms encompass a common regulatory network, including inhibition of the nuclear factor kappaB (NF-κB) signaling pathway for anti-inflammatory effects, activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2/heme oxygenase-1 (Nrf2/HO-1) signaling pathway for anti-oxidative activity, and promotion of the phosphatidylinositol-3 kinase/protein kinase B (PI3K/Akt) signaling pathway for anti-apoptosis. Concurrently, they achieve organ-specific adaptation by targeting distinct pathological features, such as modulating the neuroimmune microenvironment in the brain, optimizing cardiac energy metabolism, preserving renal microvascular integrity, targeting immune cell polarization in the liver, and maintaining intestinal epithelial barrier function and gut microbiota-immune axis homeostasis. However, their overall mechanisms and organ-specific signaling pathways remain incompletely elucidated. Therefore, this review synthesizes recent advances in SACs regarding pharmacology, pharmaceutical foundations, pharmacokinetics (PKs), and quality control. It integrates evidence supporting the “one-stone-multiple-birds” concept, critically examines key pharmaceutical challenges, and highlights future directions. Through the provision of an integrative framework, this work establishes a novel paradigm for developing multi-target natural products and provides essential theoretical support for advancing SACs toward clinical translation as a multi-disease therapeutic strategy.

title: Clostridium butyricum attenuates calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis via gut microbiota and GHDCA-VDR axis
abstract: The gut–kidney axis links the microbiota and metabolites to nephrolithiasis. We investigated the role of Clostridium butyricum (CB) in calcium oxalate (CaOx) nephrolithiasis. Metagenomics showed reduced CB abundance in patients compared with healthy controls. The CaOx crystal deposition models were induced in rats with 1% ethylene glycol; the CB group received CB bacterial powder by gavage. Micro-computed tomography (Micro-CT), biochemical assays, and histological staining demonstrated that CB mitigated renal injury and CaOx crystal deposition. 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) sequencing revealed increased gut microbial diversity and richness with CB, corroborated by fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). Untargeted and targeted metabolomics identified glycohyodeoxycholic acid (GHDCA) as a key bile acid mediating the CB effect. In vitro , GHDCA exacerbated oxalate-induced cell injury via the vitamin D receptor (VDR) in HK-2 and NRK-52E cells, which was validated in vivo using GHDCA-supplemented chow and a VDR inhibitor (ZK168281). In patients, GHDCA levels were elevated and inversely correlated with CB abundance. In summary, CB suppresses CaOx crystal deposition by modulating the gut microbiota and the GHDCA–VDR axis, supporting probiotic and small-molecule therapeutic strategies for CaOx nephrolithiasis.

title: A hypergraph convolutional neural network for cardiotoxic chemicals prediction targeting multi-channels
Organoids/Organs-on-a-Chip: A Disruptive Technology Accelerating the Arrival of the Post-Animal-Experiment Era
abstract: Traditional animal models and two-dimensional cell cultures often fail to accurately recapitulate human physiology and pathology, due to species differences, simplified microenvironments, and limited predictive power for drug responses. These shortcomings have driven the transition into the post-animal-experimentation era, demanding in vitro models with higher biomimetic fidelity. Organoids/organs-on-a-chip technologies have emerged as disruptive technologies to address these challenges. By integrating advanced assembly at the material, cellular, and functional levels, they achieve a triple-harmony of geometry-like biomimetics, cellular-type-like biomimetics, and phenotype-like biomimetics. This enables precise capture of physiological and pathological mechanisms as well as multidimensional pharmacological signatures in vitro . Here, we systematically survey the principles of construction and key characteristics of organoids/organs-on-a-chip. We then examine recent advances, current limitations, and future trends in their application to drug development, covering the cardiovascular, digestive, respiratory, and endocrine systems, as well as the major challenges that remain. A prominent consensus is that the high biomimetic fidelity of these technologies to replicate human-specific tissue architectures and disease phenotypes has most significantly accelerated progress in drug discovery, particularly in predicting efficacy and toxicity more reliably than conventional models. This disruptive technology is fundamentally revolutionizing drug development and research, ultimately providing more effective, safer, and affordable treatment options for patients around the world.

title: Gut microbiota: A key modulator of individualized efficacy and toxicity in cancer therapy
abstract: Inherent heterogeneity in response to cancer therapy remains a major clinical challenge. The composition and function of the gut microbiota are regulated by multiple factors, and its heterogeneity is a key determinant of individualized variability in therapeutic response. Accordingly, microbiota-targeted interventions combined with conventional therapies have emerged as a promising strategy for precision cancer treatment. However, comprehensive and systematic studies summarizing gut microbiota-mediated individualized response of anti-cancer therapies remain limited. To summarize current advances, we searched PubMed, Web of Science, Embase and ClinicalTrials using different combinations of keywords “gut microbiota”, “pharmacomicrobiomics”, “cancer therapy” and “personalized therapy” for studies published from January 1985 to June 2026. The available evidence shows that the gut microbiota profoundly influences tumorigenesis, cancer progression and therapeutic responses in a microbial taxon-, cancer type-, and treatment- specific manner. Specific microbial signatures may serve as predictive biomarkers for identifying patients with differential sensitivity to anticancer therapy. Moreover, gut microbiota-based interventions, when combined with standard treatments, hold considerable potential for improving therapeutic outcomes, although their clinical application remains largely exploratory. Emerging evidence also highlights important roles for intratumoral bacteria, enteroviruses and fungi in tumor progression and treatment response, providing additional opportunities for therapeutic optimization. Finally, we discuss the major limitations of current preclinical and clinical studies and outline future directions, including the integration of spatial omics technologies, large-scale randomized controlled trials and artificial intelligence assisted analyses. Collectively, this review provides a comprehensive framework for microbiota-guided precision oncology and highlights its potential to improve therapeutic efficacy and patient outcomes.

title: Advances of air-liquid interface-based microfluidic organoid chips for head and neck tumor and drug screening
abstract: Head and neck tumor is predominantly squamous cell carcinoma, originating from the paranasal sinuses, nasal cavity, oral cavity, pharynx, or larynx. These anatomical regions constitute the upper respiratory and upper digestive tracts, performing core physiological functions such as respiration and deglutition. Chronic recurrent inflammation, induced by long-term exposure to viral infections, environmental pollutants (e.g., alcohol, cigarette smoke) and high-temperature stimuli, ultimately promotes tumorigenesis. However, the high heterogeneity of tumors severely limits the efficacy of current therapeutic strategies. Currently, deciphering the microenvironmental crosstalk between cancer cells and tissue-resident cells is crucial for inhibiting tumor progression and overcoming therapeutic resistance. Similar to other tumors, air-liquid interface (ALI) model has emerged as a core technology for investigating tumor immune microenvironment, precancerous lesions, and tumorigenesis induced by environmental factors. Head and neck tumor organoid culture should enable it in vitro that closely resemble its corresponding in vivo organs with regards to immune responses, tissue organization, and physiological properties.
