Distinct from conventional models, microfluidic chips can precisely mimic the native tumor microenvironment (TME) and realize dynamic delivery of drugs and culture media. Such integrated systems support high-throughput drug screening, help overcome the limitations of traditional research models, and greatly promote the development of precision therapy for head and neck malignancies. This review summarizes the technical characteristics, applications and translational prospects of organoid, ALI culture and microfluidic platforms, aiming to provide references for preclinical research and therapeutic optimization of head and neck tumors.

title: Integrative approach combining temporal bulk transcriptomics and single-cell RNA sequencing reveals cardioprotective effects of Suxiao Jiuxin Pill on myocardial infarction
abstract: Targeting immune-inflammatory responses in myocardial infarction (MI) has emerged as a promising strategy, but the highly dynamic and complex interactions among diverse immune cell populations limit the efficacy. Suxiao Jiuxin Pill (SJP), a classical traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formulation, has been widely used to treat MI. However, the precise mechanisms of action remain poorly understood, particularly with respect to immune regulation across distinct post-infarction healing phases and at single-cell resolution. In this study, we first employed temporal bulk RNA sequencing and targeted metabolomics to delineate the transcriptional dynamics regulated by SJP during the cardiac repair process post-MI. Then, the single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was applied to comprehensively dissect the impact of SJP on the immune microenvironment of the infarcted heart. Temporal bulk transcriptomic analyses suggested that SJP promotes post-MI repair by enhancing angiogenesis, suppressing inflammation, and reprogramming myocardial energy metabolism. The scRNA-seq further revealed that SJP remodeled macrophage subset composition, enhancing both the abundance and reparative function of the Prg4 + macrophage subset. Moreover, SJP reprogrammed neutrophil subset composition and metabolic state, while restoring Treg/Th17 balance and B-cell homeostasis. Thus, the significant cardioprotective effects of SJP are primarily achieved by reprogramming the cardiac immune cell landscape after MI and facilitating the transition from inflammatory response to reparative phenotype. These findings suggest that leveraging the multi-component properties of TCM to restore the homeostasis of the cardiac immune microenvironment might provide a promising novel strategy for facilitating the transition from inflammation to tissue repair following MI.

title: Schisandrin B identified by CMC ameliorates PGN-induced immune colitis and DSS-triggered ulcerative colitis by targeting TLR2 and blocking TLR2 heterodimerization
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic intestinal inflammatory condition resulting from complex interactions. With current clinical treatments showing limited efficacy, IBD poses an increasing global health challenge. Analysis of the GEO database, clinical samples from IBD patients, and a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced murine colitis model consistently reveal elevated Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) expression at both transcriptional and protein levels, implicating it in IBD pathogenesis and highlighting its potential as a therapeutic target. Previous studies have shown that Schisandrin B (SchB) protects DSS-induced colitis, but whether it directly targets an upstream immune receptor such as TLR2, and what additional mechanisms beyond its known anti-inflammatory actions exist, remain to be explored. In this study, SchB is identified as a moderate TLR2 ligand using cell membrane chromatography (CMC). By directly binding to TLR2 and inhibiting its heterodimerization with Toll-like receptor 1 (TLR1) or Toll-like receptor 6 (TLR6), SchB exerts significant anti-inflammatory and therapeutic effects in inflammatory cell models and ameliorates both DSS-induced ulcerative colitis and peptidoglycan (PGN)-induced immune colitis in mice. SchB inhibits TLR2 signaling and activates the sequestosome 1 (p62/SQSTM1)/Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1 (Keap1)/nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) axis, concurrently exerting anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-apoptotic effects and reinforcing intestinal barrier integrity. These findings provide new evidence of molecular mechanisms supporting SchB as a promising therapeutic candidate for IBD.

title: Cyanobacteria: A sustainable platform for high-value biopharmaceutical protein production
abstract: Biopharmaceutical (therapeutic) proteins are biologically-derived drugs used to treat a variety of diseases. Producing these proteins naturally from mammalian cells presents significant challenges. As a result, non-native hosts, including plants, algae, yeast, and bacteria, have been employed to produce these proteins; however, the complex genetic reconstruction process, high cultivation costs, contamination risks, and regulatory hurdles have hampered commercial success. Cyanobacteria are a group of photoautotrophic organisms with enormous potential for sustainable manufacturing. They have recently been exploited as a potential bio-factory for therapeutic protein production. Cyanobacteria provide numerous benefits as a host for therapeutic protein production, including ease of genetic modification, cost-effective cultivation techniques, faster growth, minimal growth requirements, and low contamination risks. Successful genetic modification has enabled cyanobacteria to synthesize and accumulate diverse range of therapeutic proteins, including vaccines, antibodies, growth factors, and immunomodulatory proteins. Despite its advantages as an expression host, biopharmaceutical protein production in cyanobacteria is constrained by protein instability, low yields, and limited post-translational modification capabilities, jeopardizing its commercial viability. This review discusses various aspects of cyanobacteria-based biopharmaceutical protein production, highlighting current challenges and future prospects for overcoming them. Additionally, it analyzes the cost-effectiveness of this platform compared to other production systems.

title: The Glutamine-O-GlcNAc: A central metabolic-signaling crosstalk network in physiology and disease
abstract: Cells adapt to the environment through metabolic reprogramming, the core of which lies in the precise regulation of protein functions by converting nutritional status into functional signals. O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification acts as a unique nutrient sensor, and its only precursor, uridine diphosphate N-acetylglucosamine (UDP-GlcNAc), is synthesized via the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (HBP). This pathway integrates the metabolic fluxes of glucose, amino acids (especially glutamine), fatty acids and nucleotides. By integrating current research, this paper systematically reviews how amino acid metabolism drives the dynamic levels of the HBP and O-GlcNAc, and further explores the complex competitive and synergistic crosstalk between O-GlcNAc modification and the phosphorylation and ubiquitination systems. The results demonstrate that O-GlcNAc determines protein stability by competing with or mutually regulating phosphorylation at the same or adjacent sites, as well as by modulating the activity of E3 ligases/deubiquitinases or interfering with the phosphorylation-ubiquitination cascade, thus forming a multidimensional “metabolism-signal-homeostasis” regulatory network. This metabolism-driven core regulatory network of O-GlcNAc constitutes the central mechanism for cellular environmental adaptation, and its dysregulation is a common feature of various diseases. Intervention strategies targeting key nodes of this network, especially combinatorial targeting, provide novel insights and potential targets for metabolic intervention in the treatment of related diseases.

title: Pharmacological regulation of mitochondrial fitness and intercellular transfer mechanisms in mesenchymal stem cells for diabetic kidney disease therapy
abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD), a major microvascular complication of diabetes, is characterized by progressive renal dysfunction, wherein mitochondrial dysfunction plays a central role. Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) have emerged as a promising therapeutic platform, partly owing to their ability to transfer functional mitochondria to injured cells and restore cellular bioenergetics. However, mitochondrial transfer efficiency remains limited under pathological conditions, restricting its therapeutic potential. Recent evidence indicates that multi-component pharmacological agents can modulate mitochondrial homeostasis and cellular metabolism. In this review, we propose a mechanism-oriented framework in which pharmacological modulation enhances MSC-mediated mitochondrial transfer through coordinated regulation at three levels: i) mitochondrial fitness in donor MSCs, ii) intercellular transfer pathways, including tunneling nanotubes (TNTs), extracellular vesicles (EVs), and gap junctions, and iii) recipient microenvironment remodeling. Notably, this process can be interpreted using multiple measurable biological and bioenergetic parameters, including mitochondrial deoxyribonucleic acid (mtDNA) content, respiratory function, and redox status. From an analytical perspective, mitochondrial transfer can be assessed through quantifiable endpoints across the donor, transfer, and recipient stages, enabling a more systematic understanding of its therapeutic efficacy. This review integrates pharmacological modulation with measurable indicators of mitochondrial function and intercellular transfer to provide a framework for evaluating and optimizing mitochondrial transfer-based therapies for DKD.

title: Sufficient 2D NMR signal resolution is the precondition for achieving accurate HSQC qNMR of complex samples
Repurposing terazosin for ischemic stroke: Targeting the PTPN1/RAP1A pathway to restore neuronal mitochondrial function
abstract: Ischemic stroke (IS) remains a leading global cause of death and disability, with limited effective therapies for ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury. Drug repurposing offers a promising route for rapid clinical translation. In this study, we aimed to identify key regulatory targets involved in cerebral I/R injury and explore potential therapeutic agents for neuroprotection. Using transient middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R) in mice and cellular oxygen-glucose deprivation/reperfusion (OGD/R) models, combined with multi-omics and computational screening, we identified protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 1 (PTPN1) as a key regulator. PTPN1 was significantly upregulated in neurons after cerebral I/R injury, and neuronal PTPN1 overexpression markedly aggravated neuronal injury and neurological deficits. Mechanistically, PTPN1 enhanced the activity of Ras-related protein 1A (RAP1A) through tyrosine dephosphorylation, thereby disrupting neuronal mitochondrial function after I/R injury. Furthermore, terazosin (TZ), a drug approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (US FDA), directly bound to PTPN1, inhibited its activity, and reduced its expression by promoting SMAD ubiquitination regulatory factor 1 (SMURF1)-mediated ubiquitination. As a result, TZ alleviated neuronal mitochondrial dysfunction and improved neurological recovery after cerebral I/R injury. Thus, our work identifies the PTPN1/RAP1A pathway as a novel therapeutic target in cerebral I/R injury and establishes TZ as a potential repurposed neuroprotective agent for IS.

title: Editorial Board
Covalent inhibition of thioredoxin at K85 underlies toosendanin’s anti-hepatocellular carcinoma effects: A multi-omics perspective
Recent advances in metabolomics of mycobacteria and tuberculosis: From species differentiation to pharmacometabolomics and personalized therapy
abstract: Given its integral role in medicinal chemistry and frequent application within multi-omics strategies, metabolomics provides essential contributions to both the development of novel therapeutics and the optimization of existing drug regimens. This review presents diverse and recent applications of metabolomics closely related to Mycobacterium and tuberculosis (TB). It summarizes recent advances in metabolomics-based research which supports the understanding of the causative agent and the infection process. The applications of metabolomics cover understanding the host response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MtB) virulence, differentiation of Mycobacterium strains, uncovering the role of cellular components and networks, determination of bacterial response to stress, description of metabolites and metabolic pathways critical for early adaptive responses, understanding resistance, including the identification of drug-resistant TB, and profiling the mode of action. Moreover, pharmacometabolomics and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) show that personalized medicine may be a key in TB treatment strategy. The review summarizes pharmacometabolomic studies of first- and second-line antimycobacterial drugs, highlighting treatment-associated changes in lipid, amino acid, and energy metabolism linked to patient responsiveness, bacterial clearance, comorbid metabolic or inflammatory conditions, host genetic background, and the risk of adverse drug reactions. It will also support the future research exploring the influence of environmental and nutritional factors on bacterial metabolism and disease outcomes, which is required to deepen the understanding of the complex host-microbe interactions.

title: Nanozymes in pharmaceutical analysis: From ultrasensitive drug detection to therapeutic activity evaluation
abstract: Nanozymes are a class of biomimetic materials that integrate the physicochemical properties of nanomaterials with enzyme-like catalytic activities. As an emerging and highly promising frontier in pharmaceutical analysis, nanozymes have garnered considerable attention. Leveraging multimodal sensing and signal amplification strategies, nanozymes enable the ultrasensitive detection of trace-level drugs; meanwhile, through rational surface modification and microenvironment responsive engineering, their specificity and operational stability in complex pharmaceutical matrices have been significantly enhanced. Furthermore, nanozymes possess distinctive biological activities, positioning them as promising prodrug candidates. To provide researchers with a timely and comprehensive overview of the rapid advances in this burgeoning field, this review systematically summarizes the latest cutting-edge research progress of nanozymes in pharmaceutical analysis. We first elaborate on recent advances in nanozyme-based drug detection, encompassing innovative strategies for highly sensitive detection, enhanced specificity and anti-interference capability, and practical applications in complex pharmaceutical matrix analysis. Subsequently, we review the progress in nanozyme mediated evaluation of disease-treating activities, including efficacy assessment and mechanistic studies in antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and antitumor applications. Finally, we identify current challenges and outline future research directions. We believed that this review will inspire researchers in related disciplines and make a positive contribution to the exploration of new directions in pharmaceutical analysis.

title: 5-FUMCL: A selective and low-hepatotoxicity NLRP3 inflammasome inhibitor for treating inflammatory diseases
abstract: The activation of nucleotide-binding domain, leucine-rich repeat, and pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of numerous inflammatory conditions. Despite significant advances in the development of its inhibitors, their clinical translation remains challenging due to efficacy and hepatotoxicity concerns. We previously synthesized a new molecule, 5-FUMCL, a derivative of micheliolide, which demonstrated robust anti-inflammatory properties. Here, we report that 5-FUMCL inhibits the assembly of the NLRP3 inflammasome by interacting with the pyrin domain (PYD) of NLRP3, with W68 and P92 being critical residues for this interaction. Consequently, 5-FUMCL exhibits potent anti-inflammatory effects across various mouse models of inflammatory conditions, including peritonitis, arthritis, endotoxic shock, and diabetes, with its efficacy nullified in Nlrp3 knockout mice. Compared to MCC950, a well-established preclinical NLRP3 inhibitor, 5-FUMCL shows similar anti-inflammatory effects while exhibiting a superior hepatic safety profile upon both acute and chronic treatments. Furthermore, 5-FUMCL has proven effective in both a porcine model of endotoxic shock and a human macrophage model of NLRP3 inflammasome activation. These findings highlight 5-FUMCL as a promising inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome, distinguished by its high selectivity and low toxicity profile. This positions 5-FUMCL as a potential therapeutic agent for a wide range of inflammatory disorders in the clinic.

title: Multi-omics-informed risk stratification reveals therapeutic vulnerability to NVP-ADW742 in EGFR wild-type lung adenocarcinoma
abstract: Epidermal growth factor receptor wild-type ( EGFR WT ) lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is clinically heterogeneous, yet the biological basis underlying its divergent outcomes remains incompletely understood. By integrating multi-omics data from the EGFR WT subset of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) LUAD cohort and validation cohorts, two reproducible disease states with distinct clinical trajectories were identified. Building on this classification, a five-gene multi-omics-informed and machine-learning-based signature (MMS) was derived, which stratified prognosis across datasets, including an independent clinical cohort. The group with high MMS scores, designated as MMS high , was characterized by tumor-intrinsic malignant programs and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). MMS-based analyses further revealed therapy-relevant vulnerabilities, with MMS high models showing enhanced sensitivity to NVP-ADW742 across selected cell-line and xenograft models. Target prediction, pan-cancer characterization, and functional suppression experiments supported never in mitosis gene A-related kinase 2 (NEK2) as an MMS-linked mediator of NVP-ADW742 responsiveness. These findings collectively provide a biologically grounded framework for risk stratification and therapeutic target discovery in EGFR WT LUAD.

title: Intelligent Delivery and Regulation of Natural Polysaccharides Targeting the Gastrointestinal Barrier Network: From Local Therapy to Systemic Effects
abstract: : Oral administration is the main route for drug delivery in clinical practice. However, the bioavailability of orally administered drugs is often limited by the complexities of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Natural polysaccharides are gaining attention as oral delivery carriers because they are biocompatible and biodegradable and can interact with the GI barrier network. This review uses a framework centred on the GI barrier network to explain how the structural characteristics of polysaccharides—such as glycosidic bond type, functional groups, molecular weight, and chain conformation—determine their performance as carriers. These features enable functions including pH- and enzyme-responsive drug release, mucoadhesion, mucus penetration, transepithelial transport, and immune cell targeting. Various functional modifications can further enhance these carrier properties. In addition, reports show that natural polysaccharides and microbial metabolites can affect the "microbiota-epithelium-immune" axis through prebiotic effects. This gives them dual roles in delivery and regulation. Preclinical studies suggest that these carriers are promising for treating both local GI diseases, such as Helicobacter pylori infection, ulcerative colitis, and colorectal cancer, and systemic diseases, such as diabetes and central nervous system disorders.

title: Development of 18F-Labeled Cyclic Peptides for PET Imaging of STING Expression
abstract: The stimulator of interferon genes (STING) is a promising target for cancer immunotherapy. Developing chemically well-defined probes capable of selectively recognizing STING and transducing this recognition into quantifiable signals remains challenging. In this study, we developed and evaluated two 18 F-labeled cyclic peptide positron emission tomography (PET) radiotracers, [ 18 F]AlF-FTN-001 and [ 18 F]AlF-FTN-302, derived from the high-affinity STING ligand NNK-2. Their chemical and radiochemical properties were systematically characterized. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations, along with biolayer interferometry (BLI) and cellular uptake assays, confirmed their binding conformation, affinity, and specificity for STING. In vivo evaluation in tumor-bearing mice via PET imaging, biodistribution, and blocking studies revealed that [ 18 F]AlF-FTN-302 exhibited superior overall performance, with excellent stability, strong STING specificity, rapid tumor uptake, and high tumor-to-background contrast. Importantly, tracer uptake correlated with STING expression levels, and blocking studies validated target engagement. In conclusion, this study establishes cyclic peptides as a versatile chemical scaffold for constructing STING-targeted molecular sensors and highlights a rational strategy for tuning probe performance through subtle structural modifications. [ 18 F]AlF-FTN-302 holds significant potential for the noninvasive visualization of STING expression within the tumor microenvironment (TME).

title: Metal ions-associated redox dyshomeostasis in fibrosis: Molecular mechanisms and therapeutics
abstract: Organ fibrosis is a common pathological feature of various chronic diseases with high morbidity and mortality, and represents a major threat to global public health. The pathogenesis of organ fibrosis involves multiple etiological factors and molecular mechanisms, posing enormous obstacles to the development of anti-fibrotic drugs. In recent years, the critical role of redox dyshomeostasis in fibrogenesis has been gradually clarified. Dysregulated metabolism of metal ions such as iron, copper, zinc, and calcium induces excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, which triggers parenchymal cell injury, inflammatory responses, and fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition (FMT), ultimately leading to excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation. Thus, targeting metal ions to restore redox homeostasis has become a novel anti-fibrotic strategy. This review systematically elucidates the mechanisms by which metal ion imbalances are involved in fibrosis through oxidative stress and further provides an overview and perspective on metal ion-targeted therapeutic strategies against fibrosis.

title: Mechanistic perspectives on traditional Chinese medicine in ischemic heart disease: Focus on M2 macrophage polarization
abstract: Ischemic heart disease (IHD) poses a substantial global burden. Immune responses are pivotal in IHD progression, while the limited efficacy of conventional anti-inflammatory drugs highlights the need for dynamic modulation of the cardiac immune microenvironment. As key orchestrators, M2 macrophages determine inflammation resolution and tissue repair through efferocytosis, fibrosis modulation, and metabolic reprogramming, thereby influencing ventricular remodeling and heart failure outcomes. This review delineates the dynamic transition of cardiac macrophages from homeostasis to ischemic injury, with a focused mechanistic examination of M2 polarization and function. The effects and mechanisms of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) interventions on M2 macrophages in treating IHD are primarily centered on anti-inflammatory effects, fibrosis regulation, and metabolic reprogramming. Notably, some TCMs exhibit temporal, biphasic regulatory properties, potentially enabling balance across distinct disease stages. Future studies should deepen mechanistic insights into efferocytosis, establish dose-response relationships and safety thresholds for TCM interventions, and validate findings through high-quality clinical research.

title: Integrated scRNA-Seq and CyTOF profiling decodes multi-target immune mechanism of nucleic acid polymers restoring anti-HBs immunity in chronic hepatitis B
abstract: Among hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)-lowering strategies, nucleic acid polymers (NAPs) have demonstrated a unique ability to induce hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) humoral immunity, suggesting mechanisms beyond mere antigen reduction. To elucidate the distinct pharmacological actions of NAPs, we employed an integrated multi-omics approach in mice carrying recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 8 with 1.3 copies of the hepatitis B virus (HBV) genome (rAAV8-1.3HBV). Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) elucidated transcriptional dynamics and cell-cell communication networks, while cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) provided high-dimensional protein-level validation of immune phenotypes. We elucidated the mechanisms of NAP-induced sustained high-titer anti-HBs production. In splenic B cells, scRNA-seq revealed that NAP treatment downregulated the inhibitory receptor Fc gamma receptor II b (FCGR2B), alongside nuclear factor kappaB (NF-κB) pathway activation and germinal center (GC) formation. CyTOF confirming the expansion of activated B cell populations. In hepatic plasma cells, scRNA-seq revealed that NAP upregulated interleukin (IL)-6 signal transducer (IL6ST), enhancing interleukin 6 (IL-6) responsiveness and longevity. Furthermore, cell-cell communication analysis revealed a novel role for hepatic plasma cells in actively promoting CD8 + T cell effector differentiation, with CyTOF confirming this CD8 + T cell differentiation. Moreover, scRNA-seq revealed that NAP impaired the function of immunosuppressive cells, while CyTOF confirmed a reduction in their abundance. By integrating scRNA-seq and CyTOF, we elucidated NAP-induced multi-target immune mechanisms for sustained high-titer anti-HBs production. This study identified cooperative immune pathways critical for maintaining high-quality anti-HBs humoral immunity. Furthermore, these findings may provide insight into novel therapeutic targets for the future development of HBV immunotherapies.
